fields.h1: On the Incarnation by Athanasius: A Guide
fields.meta_title: On the Incarnation by Athanasius: A Guide
fields.description: Athanasius’s classic answers why God became man: to defeat death and restore us to God. A guide to On the Incarnation — its argument, its themes, and how to read it.
fields.body_html:
Written by a young deacon who would become one of the towering defenders of the Christian faith, Athanasius’s On the Incarnation is among the greatest short books ever written about why God became man. Composed in the early fourth century, it has never gone out of print or out of usefulness, because it answers a question every thoughtful believer eventually asks: why did the eternal Son of God take on human flesh, and what did his coming accomplish? Athanasius answers with such clarity and joy that readers across seventeen centuries have found their love for Christ enlarged. This guide introduces the book, its central argument, and how to read a work that is ancient but never dated.

Who Athanasius was, and why it matters

Athanasius (c. 296–373) served as bishop of Alexandria and became the great champion of the full deity of Christ against the teaching of Arius, who claimed the Son was a created being. So costly was his stand that he was exiled five times; the phrase “Athanasius against the world” captured his lonely faithfulness when much of the church wavered. On the Incarnation, written when he was still young, lays the groundwork for that lifelong battle by showing that only if Christ is truly God could his coming save us.

This gives the book its weight. It is not abstract speculation but the confession for which Athanasius suffered — that the one who was born in Bethlehem was the very Word of God, “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation,” by whom “all things were created” (Colossians 1:15–16). The Creator himself entered his creation. Everything else in the book flows from that.

The problem the Incarnation solves

Athanasius frames the coming of Christ as God’s answer to a genuine dilemma. God had made humanity in his own image (Genesis 1:26–27), for life and fellowship with himself. But through sin, humanity turned to corruption and death, defacing the image and falling under the sentence God had justly pronounced. Here was the divine dilemma: God’s truthfulness required that death follow sin, yet his goodness could not simply abandon the creatures he had made to ruin.

Mere repentance could not solve it, Athanasius argues, for repentance cannot undo corruption or restore what was lost. Only the Word who first made humanity could remake it; only the Author of life could conquer death. So the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), taking a body capable of death precisely so that he might die. “Since it was through man that death gained its power over men, therefore likewise it was through man” — the God-man — that death was undone (compare 1 Corinthians 15:21).

The heart of the argument: he took a body to defeat death

The core of On the Incarnation is breathtakingly simple. The Word took a human body so that, in that body, he might bear death on our behalf and destroy its power from within. “He himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14). By dying, the deathless One paid the debt of all; by rising, he broke death’s grip forever and opened the way to new life for all who are his.

Athanasius states the wonderful exchange in a famous line: “For He was made man that we might be made God.” The phrase startles modern readers, but he does not mean that we become gods by nature; he means that through Christ we are lifted into the very life of God — made his children, restored to his image, and made “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). What we lost in Adam is not merely repaired but raised higher: the Son became what we are so that we might share what he is.

Key themes to watch for

As you read, watch for the restoration of the image of God — Athanasius’s beautiful picture of humanity as a portrait spoiled and in need of the original Sitter to come and have it repainted. The Word who is the perfect image comes to renew the marred image in us. Watch, too, for the theme of recreation: the same Word who made the world at the beginning remakes it, so the Incarnation is God’s new act of creation.

Watch for Athanasius’s confidence in the resurrection and its evidences — he points to the changed lives of believers, the courage of martyrs, and the retreat of idolatry as proofs that death has truly been conquered. And notice how thoroughly Christ-centred it all is: the humility of God stooping to a manger and a cross, the Word who “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), moves Athanasius not to cold analysis but to worship.

Watch, finally, for Athanasius’s insistence that the Incarnation and the cross belong together. The Word did not take a body merely to teach or to inspire, but supremely to die — and to die a public, bodily, unmistakable death, so that his equally public resurrection might be beyond dispute. Athanasius even reflects on the manner of Jesus’ death, arguing that the Lord accepted the death others inflicted rather than choosing a private end, so that no one could doubt he truly died, and truly rose. For Athanasius the whole logic holds together: the God who could not die took a body precisely so that in it he might taste death for us and then trample it down. Remove the deity of Christ, and the whole rescue collapses; that is the truth Athanasius spent his life defending, and it beats through every page.

An ancient book rediscovered

Though it is seventeen centuries old, On the Incarnation has enjoyed a remarkable modern rediscovery, and part of the reason is a famous recommendation. A well-known twentieth-century writer, introducing a fresh translation, argued that every reader of new books should read at least as many old ones, precisely because each age is blind to its own mistakes and needs the correction of other times. Old books, he urged, are the clean sea breeze that blows through the stuffy room of contemporary assumptions — and Athanasius’s little treatise, clear and confident where modern faith is often vague and apologetic, is a bracing example.

The point is well taken. Reading On the Incarnation lifts us out of the narrow air of our own moment and sets us among believers who held the faith with a robust certainty. Athanasius does not argue nervously for a Christ he half-doubts; he expounds joyfully a Lord he would die defending. For readers weary of a thin, apologetic Christianity, this fourth-century confidence is tonic — and a reminder that the faith we hold is not a modern invention but the ancient confession of the whole church, defended at great cost long before we were born.

How to read it

Do not be intimidated by its age; On the Incarnation is remarkably readable and quite short. Read it slowly, a section at a time, and let its logic build. Because it was written to persuade, follow the argument as an argument — see how each step leads to the next — but read it also as devotion, for Athanasius means to lead you to adore the Christ he describes.

A word of counsel: read it with a Bible open, checking his reasoning against Scripture, and read the striking “made God” passage in the light of the whole book, which never confuses the creature with the Creator. Read as well the wise old advice that this ancient book is a tonic against the narrowness of any single age — for a mind fed only on the present grows small, while the great old books enlarge it. Come to Athanasius humbly, and let a bishop dead for sixteen centuries teach you to marvel again at the coming of your Lord.

Why it still speaks today

Nothing in On the Incarnation has grown stale, because its subject never will. The wonder of God becoming man, dying to defeat death, and raising us into his own life is the ever-fresh centre of the Christian faith. In an age that has largely forgotten why Christmas matters, Athanasius restores the astonishment: the Creator entered his creation to rescue it, and “the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

Read On the Incarnation for yourself and let it renew your worship. Then read it alongside the other great classics of the faith, and let this small ancient book do what it has done for countless readers before you — make the coming of Christ blaze again with meaning, and send you to your knees before the Word made flesh. Few books so short have carried so much glory, or repaid a careful reading so richly; it is the perfect place to begin reading the church fathers, and a lifelong companion once begun. Take it up, and let Athanasius teach you to wonder again at the mystery the angels announced over Bethlehem.
